tinuation then would have been: 39 B—B 4, R—B 7;
40 R—Kt 5 ch, K—B 2; 41 B—Kt 8, P—R 6;
42 P—R 5, P—R 7; 43 B × P, R × B, and if there is a win it is very difficult to find it, as against 44 P—R 6, R—R 3! offers excellent chances for a draw.

39. P × P P—R 6
40. B × Kt R × Kt P

If 40...P—R 7; 41 R—Kt 5 ch, K—R 3;
42 R—Kt 8.

41. B—Q 5 P—R 7
42. R—R 6 ch Resigns.

As an end game, this is rather a sad exhibition for two masters. The redeeming feature of the game is Rubinstein's fine combination in the middle game, beginning with 14 B × Kt.

GAME 3. IRREGULAR DEFENCE
(Havana, 1913)

White: D. Janowski. Black: J. R. Capablanca.

1. P—Q 4 Kt—K B 3
2. Kt—K B 3 P—Q 3
3. B—Kt 5 Q Kt—Q 2
4. P—K 3 P—K 4
5. Kt—B 3 P—B 3
6. B—Q 3 B—K 2
7. Q—K 2 Q—R 4
8. O—O Kt—B 1
9. K R—Q 1 B—Kt 5
